simple: the complete list of commands a processor understands, and the exact rules for writing each one.
analogy: the restaurant's ticket language that every waiter writes and the head chef reads.
precise: the interface between software and hardware: the instructions, their encodings, the registers and memory model visible to programs, and what each instruction does to that visible state. Different hardware designs can implement the same ISA.
source: D1 of F1-23 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-23 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how one particular processor design carries out the instructions of an ISA: its pipeline, caches and units.
analogy: how one kitchen is laid out and staffed to cook from the same ticket language as every other kitchen.
precise: the organisation and implementation of a processor that realises a given ISA; processors with the same ISA but different microarchitectures run the same programs with the same results at different speeds.
source: D1 of F1-23 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-23 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one command for the processor, such as "add these two numbers".
analogy: one ticket on the rail.
precise: one operation defined by the ISA, stored in memory as a binary pattern that the processor fetches, decodes and executes.
source: D1 of F1-23 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: instructions written as the bit patterns the processor really reads.
analogy: the ticket written in the kitchen's short codes.
precise: the binary encoding of a program's instructions as defined by an ISA.
source: D1 of F1-23 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: machine code written with short words and numbers so people can read it.
analogy: the ticket read aloud: "grill two salmon".
precise: a textual form of machine instructions, one line per instruction, using mnemonics such as add and register names; an assembler translates it into machine code.
source: D1 of F1-23 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D3 of F1-23 (Noam Nisan, Shimon Schocken, "The Elements of Computing Systems") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of an instruction that says which command it is.
analogy: the action word at the start of a ticket.
precise: the field of an instruction encoding that selects the operation; in U16 it is bits 15–12.
source: D1 of F1-23 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tiny, very fast storage place inside the processor that holds one value.
analogy: the chef's hands and cutting board.
precise: a named storage element that is part of the ISA's visible state; instructions name registers as sources and destinations. U16 has eight 16-bit registers, r0 to r7, and r0 always reads as 0. (The registers built from flip-flops in F1-17 are how hardware implements them.)
source: D1 of F1-23 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small number written inside the instruction itself.
analogy: "add 2 pinches of salt": the 2 is on the ticket, not fetched from a shelf.
precise: a constant operand encoded in an instruction field; U16 stores it as a 6-bit two's-complement number, so it ranges from −32 to 31.
source: D1 of F1-23 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the number that says which instruction comes next.
analogy: the clip on the ticket rail that marks the next ticket.
precise: a register holding the address of the instruction being fetched; it normally advances to the next instruction, and branches change it.
source: D1 of F1-23 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a program that turns assembly text into machine code.
analogy: the front-desk tablet that turns a spoken order into the kitchen's short codes.
precise: a translator from assembly language to machine code that also resolves labels into addresses or offsets.
source: D3 of F1-23 (Noam Nisan, Shimon Schocken, "The Elements of Computing Systems") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the parts of the processor that hold, move and change data, connected by wires.
analogy: the road one ticket takes through the kitchen: rail, cutting boards, stove, pantry hatch, shelf.
precise: the collection of functional units (ALU, register file, memories, adders, multiplexers) and the connections between them that carry out instructions, steered by control signals.
source: D1 of F1-24 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-24 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the block that holds all the registers, with doors to read two of them and write one.
analogy: the row of cutting boards beside the stove, each with a number.
precise: an array of registers with (here) two read ports, addressed by register numbers from the instruction, and one write port enabled by a control signal.
source: D1 of F1-24 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the calculator part: it adds, subtracts, compares and combines bits.
analogy: the stove, where ingredients are combined.
precise: a combinational circuit that computes one of several operations on two inputs, chosen by its operation input (built in F1-14).
source: D2 of F1-24 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a switch that picks one of several inputs to pass on.
analogy: the cook choosing whether the stove gets an ingredient from the board or a measured spoonful written on the ticket.
precise: a combinational selector whose select input, driven by a control signal, chooses which data input reaches the output (F1-12).
source: D2 of F1-24 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making a short signed number longer without changing its value.
analogy: writing "−1" on a big label instead of a small one: same value, bigger space.
precise: copying the sign bit of an n-bit two's-complement value into all higher bits of a wider word; U16 extends its 6-bit immediate to 16 bits.
source: D1 of F1-24 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a processor that does a whole instruction in one tick of the clock.
analogy: one cook who walks every ticket along the entire road before taking the next ticket.
precise: a design in which every instruction completes in one clock cycle, so the clock period must cover the longest path through the datapath.
source: D1 of F1-24 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-24 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the slowest route signals must travel before the result is ready.
analogy: the longest walk any ticket needs.
precise: the longest combinational delay between two clocked elements; it sets the minimum clock period (F1-15, F1-18).
source: D2 of F1-24 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of the processor that reads the instruction's command and switches the datapath to do it.
analogy: Amina at the pass, calling out what each station must do for this ticket.
precise: logic that maps the instruction's opcode (and sometimes other fields) to the control signals that drive multiplexer selects, write enables and ALU operation inputs.
source: D1 of F1-25 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-25 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a wire that tells one part of the datapath what to do right now.
analogy: one call such as "pantry, nothing for this one".
precise: a one-bit (or few-bit) signal such as RegWrite or AluSrcImm that selects a multiplexer input, enables a write or selects an ALU operation.
source: D1 of F1-25 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a signal that allows a storage element to change at the next clock edge.
analogy: permission to put something on a board.
precise: an input of a register, register file or memory that must be 1 for a write to happen at the clock edge; RegWrite and MemWrite are write enables.
source: D2 of F1-25 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: control built directly as logic gates.
analogy: an expediter who knows every call by heart.
precise: a control unit implemented as combinational logic (or a finite state machine) generated from the signal table.
source: D1 of F1-25 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: control that reads its calls from a small built-in table of steps.
analogy: an expediter who looks up each action word in a binder of call sequences.
precise: a control unit in which each instruction selects a sequence of microinstructions stored in a control memory; each microinstruction's bits are the control signals for one step.
source: D1 of F1-25 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D4 of F1-25 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a piece of Verilog that tests another piece by giving it inputs and printing its outputs.
analogy: a practice evening where every action word is tried once.
precise: a non-synthesisable HDL module that instantiates the design under test, drives its inputs and observes its outputs in simulation (F1-21).
source: D2 of F1-25 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: working on several instructions at once, each at a different step.
analogy: five kitchen stations in a row; at every bell each dish moves one station on.
precise: an implementation technique in which the execution of an instruction is split into stages, and successive instructions overlap, one per stage.
source: D1 of F1-26 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-26 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one step of the instruction's journey, done in one clock cycle.
analogy: one station in the row.
precise: one part of the datapath between two pipeline registers; the classic five are IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB.
source: D1 of F1-26 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a set of storage cells between two stages that holds one instruction's values for the next stage.
analogy: the tray at the hand-over between two stations.
precise: a clocked register (IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB) that captures the outputs of one stage, including the instruction's control signals, at each clock edge.
source: D1 of F1-26 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-26 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many jobs finish per unit of time.
analogy: plates out of the kitchen per hour.
precise: the rate of completed instructions, for example instructions per cycle or per second.
source: D1 of F1-26 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how long one job takes from start to finish.
analogy: the time from a ticket's arrival to its plate leaving.
precise: the time from the start to the completion of one instruction; pipelining does not reduce it and usually increases it slightly.
source: D1 of F1-26 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: on average, how many clock ticks each instruction costs.
analogy: bells per plate, averaged over the evening.
precise: total clock cycles divided by instructions executed; an ideal scalar pipeline approaches 1.
source: D1 of F1-26 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a situation where the next instruction cannot go ahead in the next cycle.
analogy: a station that cannot start because it is missing something.
precise: a condition that prevents the next instruction from executing in its designated cycle; the kinds are structural, data and control hazards.
source: D1 of F1-26 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D3 of F1-26 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not finished writing.
analogy: the fish reaches plating while the sauce is still on the stove.
precise: a dependence in which instruction j reads a register that an earlier instruction i writes, and j would read it in the pipeline before i has written it.
source: D1 of F1-27 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D3 of F1-27 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making an instruction wait a cycle, with an empty slot moving down the pipeline instead.
analogy: a station that does nothing for one bell while the rest of the row moves on.
precise: holding an instruction (and those behind it) in place for a cycle while a no-operation, the bubble, is inserted into the next stage.
source: D1 of F1-27 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: giving a result straight to the next instruction that needs it, before it is written into the register.
analogy: handing the pot across the counter instead of bottling the sauce and shelving it first.
precise: extra datapath paths and multiplexers that deliver a result from the EX/MEM or MEM/WB pipeline register to the ALU inputs of a later instruction in EX, selected by a forwarding unit that compares register numbers.
source: D1 of F1-27 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-27 (David Harris, Sarah Harris, "Digital Design and Computer Architecture") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: using a value loaded from memory in the very next instruction.
analogy: the pantry runner comes back one bell too late for the next station.
precise: a RAW hazard where the producer is a load whose value exists only at the end of MEM, so a dependent instruction immediately after it must stall one cycle even with forwarding.
source: D1 of F1-27 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: not knowing which instruction comes next until a branch is decided.
analogy: the next ticket depends on a guest's answer that has not come back yet.
precise: a hazard caused by fetching instructions after a branch before the branch outcome and target are known; wrongly fetched instructions must be flushed.
source: D1 of F1-27 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: cancelling instructions that were started by mistake.
analogy: throwing away dishes started for the wrong ticket.
precise: turning instructions already in early pipeline stages into bubbles (their control signals set to zero) so they change no state.
source: D1 of F1-27 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: putting instructions in a different order so the pipeline waits less, without changing the result.
analogy: cooking something else while the pantry runner is away.
precise: reordering independent instructions (by a compiler or by hardware) to separate producers from consumers, preserving all data dependences.
source: D1 of F1-27 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D3 of F1-27 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: guessing which way a branch will go before it is known, so the pipeline can keep going.
analogy: starting Mr Haddad's vegetables before he orders.
precise: a technique by which the processor chooses the next fetch address after a branch before the branch is resolved, and recovers (flushes) if the guess was wrong.
source: D1 of F1-28 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-28 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the cycles thrown away when a guess is wrong.
analogy: the half-grilled vegetables plus the late soup.
precise: the number of cycles lost between fetching down the wrong path and resuming at the correct one; 2 cycles for a taken branch in the model of F1-27.
source: D1 of F1-28 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a fixed guessing rule that never changes.
analogy: "always start vegetables at table seven".
precise: a prediction that does not depend on run-time history, for example always not taken, or "backward branches taken, forward branches not taken".
source: D1 of F1-28 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-28 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: guessing based on what the branch did recently.
analogy: the cook remembering what table seven ordered last time.
precise: prediction using state updated at run time with each branch's actual outcome.
source: D1 of F1-28 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a tiny counter from 0 to 3 that moves up when the branch is taken and down when it is not; 2 and 3 mean "guess taken".
analogy: the cook changes the habit only after being surprised twice in a row.
precise: a predictor state machine with four states (strongly/weakly not taken, weakly/strongly taken) that must mispredict twice in a row to change its prediction from a strong state.
source: D1 of F1-28 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-28 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small memory of predictors, one slot per branch (roughly).
analogy: a notebook with one line per table: "usually vegetables", "unpredictable".
precise: a table of prediction state (for example 2-bit counters) indexed by low-order bits of the branch's address; different branches can share an entry (aliasing).
source: D1 of F1-28 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-28 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a memory that remembers where a branch jumped to last time.
analogy: knowing not only that table seven orders, but which dish.
precise: a cache indexed by the fetch address that supplies a predicted target address, so that a predicted-taken branch can be followed in the fetch stage before decoding.
source: D2 of F1-28 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: doing work before knowing it is needed, and undoing it if not.
analogy: cooking for an order that has not arrived yet.
precise: executing instructions down a predicted path before the prediction is confirmed, without allowing them to change architectural state until it is (F1-29).
source: D2 of F1-28 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a processor that can start more than one instruction in the same clock cycle.
analogy: two grill cooks working side by side.
precise: a processor that issues several instructions per cycle to several execution units; the maximum number is its issue width.
source: D1 of F1-29 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-29 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many instructions can start per cycle at most.
analogy: how many cooks stand at the station.
precise: the maximum number of instructions the issue logic can send to execution units in one cycle.
source: D2 of F1-29 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many instructions finish per clock tick, on average.
analogy: plates out per bell.
precise: instructions completed divided by cycles; the reciprocal of CPI (F1-26). Above 1 is possible only on a superscalar processor.
source: D1 of F1-29 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many instructions in a program could run at the same time because they do not need each other's results.
analogy: eight separate salads versus one soup chain.
precise: the potential overlap among instructions of a single thread, limited by data dependences, control dependences and resources.
source: D2 of F1-29 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a line of instructions where each one needs the result of the one before.
analogy: bones → stock → soup.
precise: a path in the data-dependence graph; the longest path (sum of latencies) bounds the run time from below, however many units there are.
source: D2 of F1-29 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: running instructions as soon as their inputs are ready, not strictly in program order.
analogy: cooks starting any dish whose ingredients are ready.
precise: dynamic scheduling in which instructions wait in a window (reservation stations or an issue queue) and are dispatched when their operands are available, while results are committed in program order.
source: D1 of F1-29 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-29 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: giving each new result its own hidden register, so instructions that only reuse a register name stop blocking each other.
analogy: a fresh labelled pot per ticket instead of everyone sharing "pot 10".
precise: mapping architectural registers to a larger set of physical registers at decode, which removes write-after-read and write-after-write (name) dependences and leaves only true read-after-write dependences.
source: D2 of F1-29 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a queue that remembers the program order so results can be made official in that order.
analogy: Amina's ticket rail at the pass: plates leave in ticket order, whenever they were cooked.
precise: a circular buffer of in-flight instructions in program order; an instruction commits (updates architectural state) only when it reaches the head and has completed, which gives precise exceptions and lets mispredicted work be discarded.
source: D2 of F1-29 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one chip with several complete processors (cores) on it.
analogy: several head chefs, each with their own line, sharing a pantry.
precise: a chip containing two or more cores, each with its own pipeline and registers (and usually its own first-level caches), that share memory and usually some caches.
source: D1 of F1-30 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-30 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one running sequence of instructions inside a program; a program can have several.
analogy: one chef's list of tickets.
precise: an independent flow of control with its own registers, program counter and stack, sharing the address space of its process; the operating system schedules threads onto cores (F2-34, F3-03).
source: D3 of F1-30 (Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau, "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces"); D4 of F1-30 (ISO/IEC 14882 (the C++ standard; tier 1), sections on multi-threaded executions and data races, and the atomics library; cppreference pages for std::thread and std::atomic) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one possible order in which the steps of several threads happen.
analogy: who reads the lemon board first.
precise: a total order of the memory operations of concurrent threads that respects each thread's own order; different runs can produce different interleavings.
source: D2 of F1-30 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two threads touching the same memory at the same time, at least one writing, with nothing to keep them in order.
analogy: two chefs updating the lemon board at once.
precise: in C++, two conflicting accesses to the same memory location from different threads, at least one a write, not ordered by synchronisation and not both atomic; a program with a data race has undefined behaviour.
source: D4 of F1-30 (ISO/IEC 14882 (the C++ standard; tier 1), sections on multi-threaded executions and data races, and the atomics library; cppreference pages for std::thread and std::atomic) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an operation that happens all at once: no other thread can see it half done.
analogy: the pantry key: whoever holds it reads and writes the board before anyone else may.
precise: an operation on an atomic object that is indivisible with respect to other threads; for example std::atomic<long>::fetch_add, an atomic read-modify-write.
source: D4 of F1-30 (ISO/IEC 14882 (the C++ standard; tier 1), sections on multi-threaded executions and data races, and the atomics library; cppreference pages for std::thread and std::atomic) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the hardware's way of making sure cores do not keep using old copies of a value another core changed.
analogy: when one chef changes the board, everyone else's photo of it is torn up.
precise: a protocol that keeps the private caches' copies of each memory location consistent, usually by invalidating other copies before a write; it orders accesses to one location but does not make a read-then-write sequence indivisible.
source: D1 of F1-30 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design"); D2 of F1-30 (John Hennessy, David Patterson, "Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the part of a job that cannot be shared out limits how much faster more workers can make it.
analogy: one chef must still plate every dessert.
precise: if a fraction p of the run time can be spread perfectly over N processors, speed-up = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/N), never more than 1 / (1 − p).
source: D1 of F1-30 (David Patterson, John Hennessy, "Computer Organization and Design") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a program that turns machine code back into assembly text.
analogy: reading a kitchen's tickets aloud in words.
precise: a tool (here objdump -d) that decodes the instruction bytes in an object file or executable into mnemonics and operands, with addresses.
source: D4 of F1-31 (GNU Binutils documentation, objdump) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how hard the compiler tries to make the program fast or small.
analogy: how freely a branch may rewrite head office's recipe.
precise: a compiler option such as -O0 (no optimisation, code follows the source closely), -O1, -O2, -O3 (more aggressive transformations, including vectorisation in GCC); each enables a set of individual optimisation passes.
source: D3 of F1-31 (GNU Compiler Collection manual, "Optimize Options") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the agreed rules for where a function finds its arguments and leaves its result.
analogy: every kitchen agreeing which shelf the order slip goes on.
precise: part of the application binary interface: which registers or stack slots carry arguments and return values, which registers a function must preserve, and stack alignment; different for each ISA and operating system (F2-47).
source: D5 of F1-31 (System V Application Binary Interface, AMD64 Architecture Processor Supplement; Procedure Call Standard for the Arm 64-bit Architecture (AAPCS64); RISC-V ELF psABI (all tier 1)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a function's own scratch area in memory, made when it starts and removed when it returns.
analogy: a cook's cutting board, cleared after each dish.
precise: the region of the stack used by one function call for saved registers, local variables and spilled values, reached through the stack pointer or a frame pointer.
source: D5 of F1-31 (System V Application Binary Interface, AMD64 Architecture Processor Supplement; Procedure Call Standard for the Arm 64-bit Architecture (AAPCS64); RISC-V ELF psABI (all tier 1)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an instruction that picks one of two values depending on a condition, with no jump.
analogy: handing over plate A or plate B without walking anywhere.
precise: x86-64 cmovcc, ARM64 csel: the result depends on the flags, and the program counter goes to the next instruction in all cases, so there is nothing to predict (F1-28).
source: D1 of F1-31 (Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual); D2 of F1-31 (Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making one instruction work on several numbers at once.
analogy: one cook slicing four carrots with one stroke.
precise: transforming a loop to use SIMD instructions (for example SSE2 paddd, which adds four 32-bit integers) that process several elements per instruction.
source: D1 of F1-31 (Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual); D3 of F1-31 (GNU Compiler Collection manual, "Optimize Options") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the compiler deleting work whose result is never used.
analogy: the branch that stopped making the stock nobody tasted.
precise: an optimisation that removes computations with no observable effect; C++ allows any transformation that preserves observable behaviour (the "as-if" rule), and elapsed time is not observable behaviour.
source: D3 of F1-31 (GNU Compiler Collection manual, "Optimize Options"); D6 of F1-31 (ISO/IEC 14882 (the C++ standard; tier 1): program execution, observable behaviour and the as-if rule; undefined behaviour of signed overflow) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
